articles.title: 'Incredible': SpaceX rocket spotted off Christmas Island coast
articles.summary: A SpaceX rocket that blasted off from Texas in July, and crashed into the Indian Ocean, made an unexpected appearance off Christmas Island.
articles.body:
A SpaceX rocket has made an unexpected appearance off Christmas Island after touching down in the Indian Ocean following a test flight from Texas on 24 July.

David Watchorn, chair of the Christmas Island Tourism Association said he initially thought he was looking at ships on his way to work, before realising it was "a rocket, a space rocket" being towed.

The 52-metre long rocket has caused a stir among locals, with some "sneaking out" of work for a glimpse, and others preparing their boats for a closer look at the debris.

"It's really incredible to think about what it's been through," Watchorn told the BBC.

"The more and more you look at it, the more fascinating it's becoming".

articles.title: Artemis II: The 40 minutes when the astronauts lose contact with Earth
articles.summary: As the astronauts pass behind the Moon they will experience a moment of silence and solitude as communication with the Earth is blocked.
articles.body:
No-one will have been further from home than the Artemis astronauts.

But as the Earth shrinks ever smaller in their rear-view mirror, they've had a constant connection with mission control in Houston, Texas. The calm words from the Nasa team have given the crew a comforting link with home.

As the astronauts pass behind the Moon at about 23:47 BST (18:47 EDT) on Monday, the radio and laser signals that allow the back-and-forth communication between the spacecraft and Earth will be blocked by the Moon itself.

For about 40 minutes, the four astronauts will be alone, each with their own thoughts and feelings, travelling through the darkness of space. A profound moment of solitude and silence.

Artemis pilot Victor Glover told us he hopes the world will use the time to come together.

"When we're behind the Moon, out of contact with everybody, let's take that as an opportunity," he told BBC News before the mission. "Let's pray, hope, send your good thoughts and feelings that we get back in contact with the crew."

More than 50 years ago, the Apollo astronauts also experienced the isolation brought by a loss of signal during their missions to the Moon.

Perhaps none more so than Apollo 11's Michael Collins.

In 1969, while Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin made history taking the first steps on the lunar surface, Collins was alone in the command module, orbiting the Moon.

As his craft passed behind the far side, contact with the pair on the lunar surface, as well as with mission control, vanished for 48 minutes.

He described the experience in his 1974 memoir Carrying the Fire, saying he felt "truly alone" and "isolated from any known life", but that he did not feel fear or loneliness.

In later interviews, he described the peace and tranquillity brought by the radio silence, saying it offered a break from the constant requests from mission control.

Back on Earth, the blackout will be a tense time for those with the job of maintaining contact with the spacecraft.

At the Goonhilly Earth Station in Cornwall, in the south-west of England, a huge antenna has been collecting signals from the Orion capsule, carefully pinpointing its position throughout its journey, and feeding this information back to Nasa HQ.

Matt Cosby, Goonhilly's chief technology officer, told the BBC: "This is the first time we're tracking a spacecraft with humans on it.

"We're going to get slightly nervous as it goes behind the Moon, and then we'll be very excited when we see it again, because we know that they're all safe."

But the hope is these dropouts in communications could soon become a thing of the past. And Cosby says that will be essential as Nasa – and other space agencies around the world – begin to build a Moon base and ramp up further exploration.

"For a sustainable presence on the Moon, you need the full comms - you need the full 24 hours a day, even on the far side, because the far side will want to be explored as well," he said.

Programmes like the European Space Agency's Moonlight are planning to launch a network of satellites around the Moon to provide continuous and reliable communication coverage in the future.

For the Artemis astronauts, their time without contact with the Earth will allow them to devote all of their attention to the Moon.

They'll spend the blackout dedicated to lunar observation – taking images, studying the Moon's geology and simply gazing at its splendour.

When they emerge from the Moon's shadow, and that signal is re-established, the world will breathe a collective sigh of relief.

And the history-making astronauts will be able to share their incredible views with everyone back home.

articles.title: From blast off to splashdown: My days following Nasa's historic mission to the Moon
articles.summary: BBC Science Editor Rebecca Morelle reflects on how it felt to watch history being made.
articles.body:
For the last 10 days, four astronauts have been making history, travelling further into space than humans have been before as they voyaged to the Moon and back.

I've been following every moment of the Artemis II mission: from lift off, to their lunar close encounter and a nerve-shredding landing.

Before they blasted off into space, the crew told us that on launch day astronauts are the calmest people around.

The force of the blast passes right through you

My excitement was impossible to contain and as the rocket fired its huge boosters and engines and headed skywards, my reaction went viral.

Standing by the countdown clock at the Kennedy Space Center in Florida, alongside my BBC News science team Alison Francis and Kevin Church, was a truly visceral experience.

The burning white brightness you just can't take your eyes off, the deafening roar that takes seconds to hit you, and the force of the blast that passes right through you.

Most of all though, I just couldn't quite grasp that there were four human beings strapped into their seats at the top of a 98m-tall rocket on their way to the Moon.

As Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen got their first look at home from far above, Glover told the world: "Planet Earth, you look beautiful."

Then with a burn of their spacecraft's main engine, they said goodbye and began their quarter of a million mile journey to the Moon.

With the crew getting used to microgravity, live video was streamed back to Earth from inside their capsule.

And it was immediately clear how crammed together they were. They were living, working, eating and sleeping in a space about the same size as a minibus.

There was no privacy from each other, or from the millions of people around the world following every twist and turn.

Particular attention was paid to their Universal Waste Management System, otherwise known as the loo.

Their troublesome toilet, which cost $23m to design, had problems with its plumbing.

And we got to find out, in intimate detail, about the impact this was having on the astronauts, when questions were asked at a media briefing about the status of their "number ones and number twos".

And if you want to know - and, confession, I really did - it was "go" for "number twos" but for "number ones" collapsible contingency urine devices were deployed. Basically bags with funnels.

At the Johnson Space Center in Houston, we got to spend time in mission control - the nerve centre of the entire operation.

The team there, staring intently at their screens as data poured in, were monitoring all of the spacecraft's systems, from navigation to life support.

And this was vital. It's important not to forget that this was a test flight - the first time any humans had flown on both the rocket and the spacecraft.

And a test flight comes with real risks.

Speaking to Canadian astronaut Jeremy Hansen, for the 13 minutes presents: Artemis II podcast, while he was in quarantine before the launch really brought this home.

He told me he'd spoken to his wife and three children about the possibility that he might not come back.

Reid Wiseman also said he'd had very honest conversations with his two daughters about the dangers involved with this endeavour. He'd brought them up as a single dad after his wife died six years ago.

That loss led to one of the most poignant moments of the mission.

As the crew neared their destination, with the Moon growing ever larger in their spacecraft's window, new features became visible on the lunar surface.

They named a crater - a bright spot visible from Earth - after Reid's late wife Carroll.

The crew, all in tears, came together to hug their commander and friend. And back in Houston, there wasn't a dry eye at mission control - and that includes the BBC team.

Every single person we've spoken to at Nasa - from its head Jared Isaacman, to their fellow astronauts, and the scientists and engineers - cares deeply about this quartet, and have been rooting with every fibre of their body for them to succeed.

After breaking Apollo 13's record for the furthest distance ever travelled into space, the Artemis astronauts just kept on going.

Taking thousands of images and recording audio descriptions of the bleakly beautiful the lunar surface as it passed beneath them, the crew eventually voyaged 252,756 miles from Earth.

The legacy of Apollo runs deeply through the veins of this mission.

Messages from Apollo astronauts Charlie Duke and Jim Lovell - recorded before he died last year - were played to the astronauts during their flight.

But some have asked whether this was just a nostalgia trip. Why spend all this time, effort and money - an estimated $93bn - going back to the Moon when the US has been there already?

Nasa's administrator Isaacman told us he wants his space agency to build on Apollo, not just repeat it.

He has a raft of lunar exploration plans, from a landing planned for 2028 as well as a Moon base - and in the future he has his sights set on sending humans to Mars.

But there are also questions about whether astronauts really need to explore the Moon when orbiters, rovers and landers can do the job.

Isaac was adamant that humans must be in the mix, telling me that exploration was part of human DNA. But he also acknowledged that this came with risk.

And nowhere was this more apparent than the final challenge for the Artemis crew - their return to Earth.

It was the final challenge of their mission, and the biggest one too.

Victor Glover said re-entry was like riding a fireball through the atmosphere. And as the capsule hurtled back to Earth, it experienced temperatures half as hot as the surface of the Sun.

Watching this white-knuckle ride from mission control was an anxiety inducing experience. Especially when the communications dropped out for six very long minutes as the capsule closed in on Earth.

The relief here was palpable when a small dot of bright white light was spotted high above the ocean, and Wiseman's voice rang out at mission control, "Houston, We have you loud and clear."

With the capsule descending beneath huge parachutes to gently splashdown in the Pacific Ocean, the astronauts were back on Earth.

The focused and calm atmosphere in mission control was no more as the room erupted with celebrations. The Houston team - as well as the thousands of people who'd worked on the project - had safely brought their friends home.

The Artemis astronauts have had an extraordinary experience, which they've already acknowledged will take a long time to fully absorb.

And of course, they have an extraordinary connection with each other too.

I had the chance to speak to the crew in space as their voyage was nearing its end. I asked them what they'd miss most. Without hesitation, Christina Koch said she'd miss the camaraderie, that the crew were now like family.

They went up to space relatively unknown - now Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen have returned household names.

It does feel like we have been in the front row as history is being made. Kevin, Ali and I have been taken aback by how much this mission has gripped so many people - as we've reported around the clock to keep up with everyone's insatiable appetite for the latest news from space.

For a few brief days, the astronauts have transported millions around the world away from planet Earth - and let us ride along with them.

And if Nasa achieves its ambitious exploration plans - and other countries follow too - we'll all be back for more.

articles.title: Does 'rewilded' land need better wildfire prevention measures?
articles.summary: RSPB is considering measures it can take to improve resilience in the wake of a five week long fire
articles.body:
As we're driving in a pickup truck to see the aftermath of a huge fire which burnt for more than a month in the Cairngorms, I spot fresh smoke coming from the ground.

My guide - RSPB Scotland's site manager at the Abernethy nature reserve, Ben Oliver-Jones - puts the vehicle in reverse and we jump out to see what's happening.

It's one of several hot-spots which keeps emerging a full week after firefighters left the scene , which Ben likens to a game of whack-a-mole in an already charred landscape where the smell of burning still hangs heavily in the air.

But while the small pockets of smouldering vegetation are still being dealt with, attention is turning to improving wildfire protection.

More than 2,500 hectares of moorland and forest - about 10 square miles - was destroyed in the fire, which led to the evacuation of an entire village and where the smoke could be seen and smelt 60 miles (96.5km) away in Aberdeen.

Like a growing number of Scotland's estates, the Loch Garten and Abernethy nature reserve is being managed for ecological restoration - what others might describe as 'rewilding', a now polarising term which the RSPB avoids using.

Opponents have argued that the process leaves areas more vulnerable to uncontrollable fires, which the charity disputes, but it has identified significant land management changes it plans to make.

The changes focus on four key areas: fire breaks, wetlands, heather management and tree planting.

While the estate's network of tracks functioned as a fire break in some locations, in other areas strong winds helped high flames jump the gap.

Experts say fire from burning heather can reach heights of six metres and that fire breaks need to be three times the flame height.

RSPB Scotland says it now acknowledges that fire breaks need to be wider and has already started that process on its long network of forest trails.

Machines have been used to remove vegetation on either side of the track with the hope that what remains would not create such high flames if it were to ignite.

While it might look desolate now, the hope is that some insects and plant species will eventually colonise the ground either sides of the tracks.

It also plans to create more ponds and wet areas around the site which can be used as a source of water to pump onto fires.

A small fire on the reserve in June was extinguished using water from a pond created with cash from the Scottish government's nature restoration fund as a habitat for species like rare dragonflies.

The charity says it's working to raise water tables where bogs have been drained and create new areas of standing water for fire fighting.

Peatlands have proved problematic for wildfires because the fire can spread through the peat, deep underground as well as on the surface.

It's a problem for degraded peatland which makes up about 80% of Scotland's total, but for those in a near-natural state the peat can act as a defence.

In good condition, they keep the water level high, bringing moisture to the landscape.

Its effectiveness was demonstrated during a large fire near Melvich, Sutherland, in 2019 which reached an area that had been re-wetted 20 years earlier.

Roxane Anderson from the University of the Highlands and Islands (UNI) studied the land before and after the fire and says any damage to wet peatland was superficial and on the surface.

She argues that's a reason for accelerating peatland restoration which is currently targeting 400,000 hectares - about 1,500 square miles - by 2040 and describes it as "a complete no brainer."

"We should do it as much as we can, as quickly as we can and as strategically as we can, especially in the context of this changing climate."

On Monday, Scotland's chief fire officer published an open letter calling for better wildlife planning and urging a "more formal and proportionate fire safety regime" to match that for businesses in urban settings.

It comes as the Scottish government enters the final stages of introducing licences for muirburn - the controlled burning of heather on moorland primarily managed for grouse shooting.

Ministers have brought in the licences to make moorland more "environmentally sustainable", but Scottish Land and Estates say the practice is a valuable tool for reducing vegetation which can act as fuel to a wildfire.

RSPB Scotland does not practice muirburn but accepts that the "fuel load" does need to be managed.

It has been doing that through grazing cattle, which eat the vegetation, while in other areas land managers have used machines to cut and mulch the grass, gorse, bracken and heather.

While some sporting estates remain opposed to "rewilding", others have embraced some of the elements of ecological restoration.

The Rottal estate in the Angus Glens has been working with the RSPB for several years now and owner Dee Ward believes there is a lot of common ground.

He has been re-wetting peatland, planting trees and encouraging wading birds and says that while the "ideological extremists" have been holding the narrative, a lot more estates are trying to find the middle ground.

He added: "There are people that are very anti-grouse shooting. Fair enough, that's your choice. But that's clouding their view about muirburn because they're saying because grouse shooters do it, it must be bad."

Dee urges both sides to begin looking at land management practices through the lens of preventing wildfires and consider sharing appropriate methods.

The fourth move RSPB Scotland plans is the introduction of more broadleaved trees in its woodlands.

It says that while pines contain flammable resins, species such as alder, rowan, aspen and birch are higher in moisture content which means they do not burn as easily.

Abernethy hosts the largest and most important remnant of Scotland's ancient Caledonian pine forest and so the Scots pines are an important part of the mix.

But the charity wants to explore the option of increasing the proportion of other species, which would have occurred naturally in the original forest anyway.

Michael Bruce, owner of the Glen Tannar estate in Aberdeenshire, specialises in controlled burning of moorland and helps the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service with its wildfire forecasting.

He says that there hasn't been enough academic research and modelling in the UK on how wildfires behave to make land management changes meaningful.

While two significant studies have been carried out in Scotland over the past 25 years, neither has been long-term or consistent and he believes events of the summer demonstrate the need for improved understanding.

He believes there is no silver bullet which will prevent a wildfire starting or spreading but that estates "need to build up layers of defence".

Firms affected by Cairngorms wildfire offered support from £3m fund

'Apocalyptic' damage as Cairngorms wildfire burns for two weeks

In April, the Cairngorms National Park Authority introduced a bylaw making it illegal to start a fire or a BBQ during the summer months to prevent wildfires.

Despite the huge blaze, figures suggest that move has been effective at reducing potential sources of ignition, with the number of campfires or barbecues recorded so far this year totalling 36 compared with 94 in the same period last year.

That's still too many but the reduction perhaps emphasises the importance of preventing a fire's spread.

Wildfires have been described to me as an "intermittent problem" because they're seasonal and we don't see large ones happening every year.

If they happened every year, it would become an obvious priority.

Preventing and tackling them both cost money and there are obvious questions around striking the balance between spending on both, not to mention wider affordability.

But climate change is predicted to bring more long, dry spells which create the tinderbox of summer 2026 and so all of this may be seen as an investment in the future.

For five weeks, land managers with very opposing views on how the uplands should be managed stood side by side battling the enormous blaze which was sweeping through the Cairngorms.

They found a common purpose and it's hoped that now seeing the countryside through a prism of wildfire risk may now be the unifier which sees them exchanging at least some practices - even if their end goals for the landscape still differ wildly.

articles.title: Photos: Scientists take to the skies and spot more than 2,000 species at marine monument
articles.summary: New England scientists observed more than 2,000 animals during a recent aerial survey over the Northeast Canyons and Seamounts Marine National Monument, high...
articles.body:
The New England Aquarium observed more than 2,000 animals during an aerial survey.

At the start of the survey, scientists counted about 1,800 dolphins across four species.

The team also spotted an endangered blue whale and a small group of endangered fin whales.

New England scientists observed more than 2,000 animals during a recent aerial survey over the Northeast Canyons and Seamounts Marine National Monument, highlighting the area's diverse wildlife .

See It: Stingrays Make Surprise Appearance In Polluted New York City Waterway

A team from the New England Aquarium 's Anderson Cabot Center for Ocean Life flew over the area in a survey aircraft on Aug. 16 and recorded 15 different marine species during the flight.

"The diversity of sightings was truly remarkable and a testament to why the monument is such a special habitat," Katherine McKenna, an associate research scientist at the aquarium's Anderson Cabot Center, said.

At the start of the survey, scientists counted about 1,800 dolphins across four species. They later documented a sperm whale, humpback whale, 11 whale sharks, manta rays, Chilean devil rays and hammerhead sharks.

From Manatees To Mammals, Zoo Animals Turn To Acupuncture For Specialized Care

"From regular visitors like dolphins and sperm whales, to large baleen whales drawn by aggregations of zooplankton and whale sharks and manta rays following warm Gulf Stream waters, the monument brings together an incredible variety of marine life," McKenna said.

Meet The Rare Two-headed Gecko That Is Going Viral For Defying The Odds

The team also spotted an endangered blue whale and a small group of endangered fin whales, including a mother and calf feeding just outside the monument.

"Seeing a variety of threatened and endangered species actively feeding in the monument was particularly memorable and underscores the importance of protecting this productive habitat," McKenna said.

The New England Aquarium's previous flight over the monument took place on July 13, 2026. During that survey, the team identified nearly 650 animals, including more than 600 dolphins, four endangered sperm whales, 23 pilot whales and a whale shark.

Great White Shark Quint Arrives At Key Seasonal Habitat Near Cape Cod

The monument was established in 2016 as an underwater sanctuary. The nearly 5,000-square-mile area is located about 130 miles southeast of Cape Cod .

The area contains three deep-sea canyons that provide habitat and feeding grounds for a vast array of marine species.

Earlier this year, the Trump administration rolled back protections for the monument, allowing commercial fishing in the area.

The change has raised concerns among conservationists about how increased fishing activity could affect the diverse marine life that relies on the monument.

articles.title: In Guam, scientists trace a snake invasion from a few stowaways to 30,000 per square mile
articles.summary: Instead of being undone by inbreeding, the species prospered.
articles.body:
A snake population that could have been expected to die out quickly became one of Guam's most destructive invasive species.

New genome research from the University at Buffalo is helping explain how brown tree snakes — descended from only a few accidental arrivals — reached densities of up to 30,000 per square mile.

The paper , published in Science Advances on July 24, found more than 19,000 structural variants in the brown tree snake genome.

Those results offered a possible explanation for how just a few founding snakes endured an extreme genetic bottleneck and still spread throughout Guam.

Many of those genomic differences were found in genes linked to immune function and scent, traits that may have helped the snakes adapt to unfamiliar conditions.

That is notable because invasive populations that start with very limited genetic diversity are usually expected to be at a disadvantage.

The researchers said the species' strong sense of smell may even enable individuals to tell close relatives apart from potential prey.

In broader terms, the study indicates that heavy inbreeding may not eliminate as much adaptive capacity as scientists once assumed.

Although brown tree snakes are native to Australia and the South Pacific, they are believed to have been introduced to Guam by human activity, potentially arriving as hidden passengers on cargo aircraft after World War II.

Once established, they devastated Guam's native forest birds and altered the island's ecology.

They also created a persistent infrastructure problem by climbing utility poles and causing hundreds of power outages each year.

Most striking is that this invasion grew from only a small number of original snakes into populations topping 30,000 per square mile.

Instead of being undone by inbreeding, the species prospered.

One of the biggest advances is a better understanding of the invader itself.

By mapping the structural quirks of the brown tree snake genome, researchers have given scientists and wildlife managers new clues about why this species succeeded where a tiny introduced population might have been expected to fail.

That could help sharpen future control strategies by allowing experts to focus on the biological traits that made the snakes so resilient.

If scent and immune-system genes played a major role in their spread, those pathways may become especially important targets for future monitoring and research.

The result may also be encouraging for endangered animals that have suffered major population crashes, as it suggests adaptive potential that can persist even in inbred groups.

Guam's snake crisis appears to have begun with human transport, and the longer an invasive species has to establish itself, the harder and more expensive it becomes to contain the damage.

Guam's blackout-causing snake problem shows how a few unintended passengers can permanently alter an ecosystem, and new research shows how unexpectedly durable those populations can be once they arrive.

articles.title: California releases more than 3,000 endangered mountain frogs into the wild, restoring a species that has lost most of its home
articles.summary: Science News: More than 3,000 endangered mountain yellow-legged frogs and tadpoles have been released into Californiaâs mountain ranges in 2026, giving a once wides.
articles.body: More than 3,000 endangered mountain yellow-legged frogs and tadpoles have been released into Californiaâs mountain ranges in 2026, giving a once widespread amphibian another chance to survive in the wild. The reintroduction, carried out by the âSan Diego Zoo Wildlife Allianceâ and its partners, is part of a long-running effort to rebuild populations of a species that has suffered a dramatic decline. The tiny frogs have been returned to high-elevation habitats in the San Bernardino and San Jacinto mountains. Their release marks another step in a conservation programme that began as a rescue effort and has now returned more than 10,000 mountain yellow-legged frogs to the wild. The work also highlights how carefully managed breeding, monitoring and habitat restoration can help endangered wildlife regain a foothold in its native home.How are 3,000 frogs being returned to the Californian mountainsThe latest releases are part of a conservation breeding and reintroduction programme led by the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance. According to PEOPLE, more than 3,000 mountain yellow-legged frogs and tadpoles have been reintroduced during 2026 into the San Bernardino and San Jacinto mountains, areas within the speciesâ historic range. Some were released into high-elevation habitats including Bluff Lake in the Big Bear Valley. The programme began in 2006 as a simpler rescue effort before developing into a broader breeding and reintroduction project. The frogs released this year were bred at the organisationâs Beckman Center for Conservation Research before being moved back into suitable mountain habitats.The San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance explains that its conservation team has been working to improve breeding methods so that more healthy young frogs can eventually be returned to the wild. Scientists recreate conditions that frogs experience naturally, including seasonal changes and colder periods that encourage hibernation. They also adjust light cycles and study the animalsâ nutritional needs. Because natural breeding remains difficult, the organisation has also explored assisted reproductive methods, including hormone treatments and in-vitro fertilisation(IVF). At the same time, sperm is preserved through its âFrozen Zoo programmeâ to help protect the speciesâ genetic diversity for the future.Reason for mountain yellow-legged frogs becoming so rareMountain yellow-legged frogs once played a major role in the high-country ecosystems of Californiaâs Sierra Nevada. According to the National Park Service (NPS), âRana muscosaâ and âRana sierraeâ live in naturally fishless lakes, ponds and streams at high elevations. They were once the most numerous amphibians in the Sierra Nevada, but have disappeared from 92% of their historic range. The decline has been severe enough for both species to receive legal protection. The NPS says Rana muscosa was listed as endangered and Rana sierrae as threatened under Californiaâs Endangered Species Act in 2012. Both were later listed as endangered under the federal Endangered Species Act in 2014.One of the biggest problems came from an unexpected change to mountain lakes. Trout were introduced into high-elevation waters to attract people interested in fishing and recreation. The fish eat tadpoles and young frogs and also compete with them for insects. According to the NPS, trout can force frogs into smaller, poorer-quality areas and separate populations from one another. A deadly fungal disease known as chytridiomycosis has added another major threat. The disease attacks the skin of frogs and can kill infected animals, making it particularly damaging to populations already weakened by other pressures.What has conservation work achieved so farSan Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance has now reintroduced more than 10,000 mountain yellow-legged frogs into the wild, including the animals released during 2026. The frogs are being monitored after release to track their health, survival and ability to establish themselves in their native habitats. There is evidence from other restoration work in California that mountain yellow-legged frogs can respond strongly when some of the pressures facing them are reduced. The NPS describes a restoration programme in Sequoia and Kings Canyon National Parks where staff began removing introduced trout from selected lakes and streams in 2001. Using large nets and equipment that temporarily stuns fish, park staff removed nearly 44,000 fish from 19 lakes by 2011, including complete removal from nine lakes. The results were striking. In three Upper LeConte Canyon restoration lakes, surveys found that the number of frogs and tadpoles increased from nearly 190 in 2001 to more than 18,800 in 2004 after most of the fish had been removed. More than 2,000 frogs also moved into two nearby lakes.Importance of bringing the frogs back from the brinkThe recovery of mountain yellow-legged frogs is important not only because it could prevent an endangered species from disappearing. The frogs are also part of a wider mountain food chain. The NPS explains that frogs eat insects such as grasshoppers and are themselves eaten by animals including snakes and hawks. Their disappearance can therefore affect other wildlife and disturb the natural balance of mountain ecosystems. Introduced trout can also consume aquatic insects and other small animals, creating additional changes in these habitats.The challenge, however, is far from over. The San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance lists disease, non-native predators, wildfire, drought, habitat destruction, pollution and agriculture among the threats facing the species. Its conservation programme focuses not simply on producing frogs, but on giving them a better chance of surviving once they leave human care. Their future will depend on whether they survive, reproduce and establish new generations in the wild. For now, the growing number of releases offers conservationists a reason for cautious optimism that with sustained care, a species once common across Californiaâs mountains may have a path back.

articles.title: Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026 â the best pictures so far
articles.summary: The polar bear image taken by Audun Rikardsen was among the 'highly commended' entries in this year's competition.
articles.body:
How would it feel to find yourself face to face with one of the Arctic's most formidable predators?

This stunning image captures life from a seal's perspective. Taken by Norwegian wildlife photographer Audun Rikardsen, it was among the 'Highly Commended' entries in this year's Wildlife Photographer of the Year competition.

While working as a guide with Arctic Wildlife Tours, Rikardsen rigged an underwater camera with a motion sensor beneath a seal's breathing hole, and then waited. At 4am, a female polar bear approached and peered down.

Rikardsen then waited eight hours for the bear to move away before retrieving the camera and reviewing the images.

When he saw what he had captured, he said: "I was so extremely happy. I was screaming, so I probably woke up all the polar bears for miles."

Rikardsen has previously won two Wildlife Photographer of the Year categories: Birds in 2019 and Oceans: The Bigger Picture in 2025 .

The overall winners will be announced on Tuesday 13 October 2026, followed by an exhibition at the Natural History Museum in London , external from Friday 16 October 2026.

Scroll down to explore other highly commended works from the competition.

Living alongside polar bears in the Canadian Arctic - BBC World Service

Crockford watched swifts return to London after their annual migration from Africa, filling the air with their high-pitched calls. Most flew too high to photograph, but a few lower-flying ones gave Crockford the opportunity to capture the picture he wanted.

Swifts spend almost their entire lives in the air, usually landing only to nest.

After rainfall, Miyazawa came across an Eastern Japanese toad making its way along a city street. He used a slow shutter speed to photograph it before it hopped back into the bushes.

Eastern Japanese toads are typically found in forests, grasslands and other terrestrial habitats across eastern Japan, but they have also proved remarkably adaptable to urban environments.

Photographer: Vegard Byrkjeland Aasen (Norway)

Category: Highly Commended, Behaviour: Mammals

Location: Kvænangen, Troms County, Norway

Aasen was flying a drone for the Norwegian Orca Survey when he noticed an adult orca carrying the body of a deceased calf through a Norwegian fjord.

The orca repeatedly allowed the calf to sink before bringing it back to the surface, a difficult moment to watch but one that Aasen felt was important to record.

The behaviour may have been an attempt to revive or protect the calf. Killer whales have previously been observed carrying deceased calves, including a case where a female Southern Resident killer whale carried her dead calf for at least 17 days.

A 2026 study , external suggests that this type of behaviour may be more widespread across the species than previously thought.

Photographer: Andrea & Maceo Grammatico (France)

Category: Highly Commended, Animal Portraits

Location: Sierpe, South Puntarenas, Costa Rica

Only when they reviewed the images did the Grammatico twins realise they had captured a mosquito resting on the head of a fer-de-lance viper. They described it as "one of the most demanding focus stacks we've ever created".

Highly venomous and responsible for more fatal snake bites in Central America than any other species, the fer-de-lance is well camouflaged and can blend into plantation habitats, sometimes going unnoticed by workers.

Location: Meeting of the Waters State Park, Northern Pantanal, Brazil

Parkinson photographed a black vulture perched over a dead yacaré caiman in Brazil's Pantanal wetlands, keeping his boat at a distance and using a long telephoto lens to capture the shot.

A jaguar waiting out of frame emerged after the vulture flew away to claim the carcass. Only then did Parkinson notice a suspiciously clean, straight wound on the back of the caiman's head, possibly caused by a blow from a speeding boat, he suspects.

Photographer: Dewald Tromp (South Africa)

Category: Highly Commended, Animals in their Environment

Location: Namib Desert, near Swakopmund, Namibia

Tromp was photographing a Namaqua chameleon in the Namib Desert when the wind suddenly intensified, bringing a sandstorm that quickly reduced visibility and made breathing difficult.

These chameleons are desert specialists and can obtain moisture directly from the air. Dew gathers on their skin and is channelled towards their mouths through microscopic grooves, while their tongues can also collect fog water condensed on plants, sand and rocks.

Photographer: Bence Máté (Hungary) - 2010 Wildlife Photographer winner

Category: Highly Commended, Behaviour: Birds

Location: Ashnil Aruba Lodge, Tsavo East National Park, Kenya

Máté was watching birds gather at a small pond when tens of thousands of red-billed queleas swept down to drink in the golden late-afternoon light. The movement of so many wings created a rush of air that, he says, could be felt from 30m (98ft) away.

Red-billed queleas can gather in flocks of up to two million and are considered the most abundant wild bird on Earth, with an estimated 1.5 billion breeding adults.

Photographer: Ernest Porter (South Africa)

Location: Manyeleti Game Reserve, Mpumalanga, South Africa

While searching the reserve for wildlife, Porter photographed a red-billed oxpecker rubbing its bill against a white rhino's skin in the afternoon light. The birds feed on insects living on rhinos and can also act as sentinels - calling to warn their hosts when danger approaches. In Swahili, the red-billed oxpecker is known as askari wa kifaru, meaning "the rhino's guard".

Hutton had watched a young leopard pursue a squirrel into a tree, having earlier seen the cat unsuccessfully attempt to stalk a rabbit. The squirrel escaped by climbing higher, leaving the leopard clinging on before it eventually made an awkward retreat.

For young leopards, survival is far from guaranteed: fewer than half reach independence, with male leopards, lions and other predators among the threats they face.

Category: Highly Commended, Behaviour: Amphibians and Reptiles

Location: Central Kalahari Game Reserve, Botswana

An African bullfrog lunges for a babul butterfly but misses.

Cullmann had noticed tadpoles on a previous visit after heavy rains and returned the following month to find ponds and puddles full of young bullfrogs. He spent more than two weeks watching the young frogs "eat everything that moved".

As adults, African bullfrogs can reach 12cm (4.7in) in length and spend around 10 months of the year dormant underground, emerging after the rains to breed and feed voraciously.

Category: Highly Commended, Behaviour: Invertebrates

Location: Wildsumaco Biological Station, Napo Province, Ecuador

Wizen was photographing a lichen dragon katydid measuring just 15mm long, making it difficult to distinguish from the lichen around it. He spotted the insect when it moved, but even then struggled to separate it from its background through the viewfinder.

Found only in Ecuador's Andes Mountains, its spiny armour helps protect it from eagle-eyed predators that can see through its disguise.

Photographer: Shane Gross (Canada) - 2024 Wildlife Photographer winner

Category: Highly Commended, Oceans: The Bigger Picture

Gross was photographing a school of bigeye trevally near the shore at sunrise as a storm approached. To create a split-level image, he turned his camera upside down to aid buoyancy distribution and slowly moved towards the curious fish.

Bigeye trevally are fished in many parts of the world, but here they are relatively safe. In 2023, the waters surrounding D'Arros Island were made a Marine Protected Area and designated as a no-take zone as part of the worldwide initiative for governments to protect 30% of Earth's land and ocean by 2030.

Category: Highly Commended, Urban Wildlife

Elliott spent hours watching through the kitchen window of a local resident's home, hoping to photograph black bears that frequently pass through the garden. He observed one stopping for a dip in the garden pool, highlighting the increasingly common overlap between wildlife and residential life in Los Angeles County, where housing developments have spread into bear habitat.

Photographer: Ralph Pace (USA) - 2025 Underwater category winner

Category: Highly Commended, Wetlands: The Bigger Picture

A sea hare glides through an eelgrass meadow in the shallows of Monterey Bay, where Pace was photographing in the evening light. He saw the encounter as a hopeful image of "a gentle giant safeguarding the last green meadows of the sea".

By grazing on red algae, that can prevent sunlight reaching the meadow, sea hares play a role in restoring eelgrass, which is vital to coastal ecosystems and an important carbon sink.

Category: Highly Commended, Photojournalism

After learning that a circus featuring animal acts was in town, Rojas went to document it and saw a brown bear riding a small motorcycle, muzzled and secured to the apparatus. For him the scene highlighted the contrast between the animal's wild nature and the human environment imposed upon it.

More than 50 countries around the world have now banned or restricted the use of wild animals in circuses, over concerns it causes them distress , external .

Wildlife Photographer of the Year is developed and produced by the Natural History Museum, London.

articles.title: Entenda por que o eclipse lunar desta semana não será uma 'Lua de Sangue' | G1
articles.standfirst: Fenômeno poderá ser visto em todo o Brasil entre a noite de quinta-feira (27) e a madrugada de sexta (28). Lua poderá ganhar tons avermelhados, mas não ficará totalmente vermelha durante o eclipse.
articles.summary: Fenômeno poderá ser visto em todo o Brasil entre a noite de quinta-feira (27) e a madrugada de sexta (28). Lua poderá ganhar tons avermelhados, mas não ficará totalmente vermelha durante o eclipse.
articles.body:
Um eclipse lunar parcial é visto atrás da antena no topo do One World Trade Center na cidade de Nova York (EUA). — Foto: Eduardo Munoz

Na noite de quinta-feira (27) para sexta-feira (28) , o céu vai reservar um eclipse lunar parcial que promete chamar atenção em todo o Brasil.

A Lua ficará quase toda encoberta pela sombra da Terra, num fenômeno que poderá ser visto a olho nu e sem qualquer equipamento especial .

O eclipse começará às 22h24 de quinta-feira e seguirá pela madrugada. O ponto máximo será às 1h13 de sexta (28), quando 96,2% do disco lunar estará escurecido.

📱Favorite o g1 no Google e acompanhe as principais notícias do dia

Embora seja visualmente muito próximo de um eclipse total, o fenômeno será parcial .

Isso porque somente uma pequena parte da Lua ainda ficará fora da umbra , a região mais escura da sombra da Terra.

E como a Lua não entrará completamente na umbra, ela poderá até ganhar tons avermelhados durante parte do eclipse, mas não ficará totalmente vermelha .

“Quando temos um eclipse total, quanto mais alinhados eles estão, mais tempo ela fica na umbra. Já neste caso, ela não mergulha totalmente nessa região, então vai começar a ficar avermelhada e, logo depois, vai deixar de ficar avermelhada”, explica Josina Oliveira do Nascimento, astrônoma do Observatório Nacional (ON).

(veja no INFOGRÁFICO abaixo como a Lua vai atravessar a sombra da Terra durante o eclipse).

Abaixo, entenda também o que é um eclipse lunar, veja os horários de cada fase e saiba como acompanhar o fenômeno.

Durante um eclipse lunar, é a sombra da Terra que obscurece a Lua.

O fenômeno acontece quando Sol, Terra e Lua ficam alinhados, com a Terra posicionada entre os outros dois astros .

➡️ A sombra projetada pela Terra no espaço tem duas regiões: a penumbra , mais clara, e a umbra , mais escura.

Quando a Lua passa apenas pela penumbra, ocorre um eclipse penumbral , normalmente mais difícil de perceber a olho nu.

Já no eclipse parcial , uma parte da Lua entra na umbra.

No total , todo o disco lunar fica dentro dessa região mais escura.

Na madrugada de sexta-feira, a Lua entrará profundamente na umbra, mas não por completo.

Por isso, durante o ponto máximo do fenômeno, será possível observar uma pequena faixa ainda iluminada e quase todo o restante do disco lunar coberto pela sombra da Terra.

Diagrama mostra a diferença da umbra e da penumbra. — Foto: NASA

O eclipse começará ainda na noite de quinta-feira (27) e terminará somente na madrugada de sexta-feira (28).

Veja os horários abaixo (no horário de Brasília):

1h13 (28/8): ponto máximo do fenômeno, quando ocorre o maior obscurecimento;

A fase parcial, que é a mais facilmente perceptível, terá duração de aproximadamente 3 horas e 18 minutos .

Considerando também as etapas penumbrais, o eclipse completo se estende por cerca de 5 horas e 38 minutos .

☝️ Ou seja: se você quiser acompanhar o momento em que quase toda a Lua estará encoberta terá de olhar para o céu à 1h13 da próxima sexta-feira (28), e não na madrugada de quinta-feira.

Em estados com fusos diferentes do horário de Brasília, os horários precisam ser ajustados.

Em áreas no fuso de uma hora a menos, por exemplo, o ponto máximo ocorrerá à 0h13 .

Como este não será um eclipse total, a Lua não ficará completamente avermelhada como ocorre na chamada “ Lua de Sangue ”.

Mesmo assim, a parte do disco lunar que estiver dentro da umbra poderá adquirir tons mais escuros, alaranjados ou avermelhados .

Isso acontece porque parte da luz do Sol atravessa a atmosfera terrestre antes de chegar à Lua.

A luz azul se espalha com mais facilidade na atmosfera, enquanto comprimentos de onda mais longos, como os tons vermelhos e alaranjados, conseguem atravessá-la e alcançar a superfície lunar.

É o mesmo processo que ajuda a explicar os tons avermelhados do nascer e do pôr do Sol .

A Nasa compara o fenômeno a todos os amanheceres e entardeceres da Terra sendo projetados sobre a Lua.

"É o mesmo fenômeno que torna o pôr do Sol vermelho. É como se a luz do Sol fosse filtrada pela nossa atmosfera e sobrasse esse vermelho que espalha a luz do Sol que incide sobre a Lua", diz Alessandra Abe Pacini, cientista do grupo de Física Espacial da Universidade do Colorado.

O fenômeno da Lua de Sangue — Foto: Arte/g1

Nenhum equipamento especial é necessário para observar o eclipse. O fenômeno poderá ser visto a olho nu e, ao contrário de um eclipse solar, não oferece risco à visão.

“Para ver o eclipse da Lua não é preciso nenhum aparato, basta olhar e contemplar pelo tempo que quiser”, afirma Josina.

🔭 Binóculos ou telescópios podem melhorar a visualização dos detalhes da superfície lunar e da região coberta pela sombra.

O principal obstáculo será mesmo o tempo: nuvens podem impedir ou dificultar a observação.

O eclipse também será visível em outras partes da América, além de regiões da Europa e da África.

No Brasil, porém, será possível acompanhar todas as fases do fenômeno, da entrada da Lua na penumbra até o fim do eclipse, já perto das 4h da manhã de sexta-feira.

No eclipse total, a luz azul do Sol se espalha e a luz vermelha, laranja e amarela (de comprimento de onda mais longo) atravassa, tornando nossa Lua vermelha. — Foto: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center/Scientific Visualization Studio

( VÍDEO: Vídeo mostra timelapse do eclipse lunar parcial mais longo visto em Tóquio.)

articles.title: Fóssil de peixe de 254 milhões de anos revela nova espécie em MT | G1
articles.standfirst: Exemplar de cerca de 15 centímetros está quase completo e ajuda a mostrar como eram os peixes que viviam na região pouco antes da maior extinção em massa conhecida da história da Terra.
articles.summary: Exemplar de cerca de 15 centímetros está quase completo e ajuda a mostrar como eram os peixes que viviam na região pouco antes da maior extinção em massa conhecida da Terra.
articles.body:
Fóssil de Leolepis matogrossensis, nova espécie de peixe que viveu há cerca de 254 milhões de anos onde hoje é Mato Grosso. O exemplar é o único conhecido da espécie e está preservado quase por inteiro. — Foto: Reprodução/Journal of South American Earth Sciences

Um pequeno peixe que viveu onde hoje é Mato Grosso há cerca de 254 milhões de anos foi identificado como uma espécie até então desconhecida pela ciência.

Batizado de Leolepis matogrossensis , o animal media aproximadamente 15 centímetros e teve quase todo o corpo preservado.

📱Favorite o g1 no Google e acompanhe as principais notícias do dia

O achado é considerado raro porque fósseis de peixes dessa época encontrados no Brasil costumam aparecer apenas em partes, como dentes, escamas e fragmentos de ossos.

O estudo, publicado em julho no "Journal of South American Earth Sciences", aponta que esse é o peixe do Permiano (último período geológico da Era Paleozoica) mais bem preservado já encontrado em Mato Grosso.

O Leolepis viveu em uma região ocupada por um grande ambiente de água doce . Com o fóssil quase completo, os pesquisadores conseguiram analisar partes do crânio, das mandíbulas e das escamas e comparar o animal com outros peixes antigos.

“Por estar excepcionalmente preservado, o exemplar pode ajudar os pesquisadores a reconhecer a presença da espécie em outras áreas da Bacia do Paraná e a estabelecer novas correlações entre diferentes formações geológicas”, disse Valéria Gallo, pesquisadora da Universidade do Estado do Rio de Janeiro (UERJ) e uma das autoras do estudo, em um comunicado.

O peixe viveu no fim do Permiano, pouco antes da maior extinção em massa conhecida da história da Terra, ocorrida há cerca de 252 milhões de anos .

Nesse evento, mais de 70% das espécies terrestres e cerca de 94% das espécies marinhas desapareceram, segundo os dados citados no estudo. As principais hipóteses científicas relacionam essa crise ambiental a grandes episódios de atividade vulcânica.

O fóssil também foi encontrado em uma região que chama atenção por outro motivo: o local fica a cerca de 50 quilômetros da cratera de Araguainha , entre Mato Grosso e Goiás.

Com aproximadamente 40 quilômetros de diâmetro, ela é considerada a maior e mais bem preservada estrutura de impacto conhecida na América do Sul. A cratera foi formada pela colisão de um asteroide estimado em 2 a 3 quilômetros de diâmetro.

Apesar da proximidade, o estudo não aponta o impacto como causa da grande extinção do fim do Permiano. Os autores afirmam que o Leolepis viveu antes da colisão e que as rochas onde o fóssil foi encontrado não foram diretamente alteradas pelo evento.

O exemplar foi coletado em 2005 pelo geólogo Léo Adriano de Oliveira e hoje faz parte da coleção paleontológica da Universidade Federal de Mato Grosso (UFMT), em Cuiabá.

O nome da nova espécie também faz referência à história do achado: Leolepis homenageia Léo Adriano de Oliveira, enquanto matogrossensis remete ao estado onde o fóssil foi encontrado.

articles.title: Emerging threat discovered in Colorado River in Utah for first time
articles.summary: An aquatic invasive species that has emerged as a threat in the Upper Colorado River basin has now become a growing concern on the river in Utah.
articles.body:
An aquatic invasive species that has emerged as a threat in the Upper Colorado River basin has now become a growing concern in the Colorado River in Utah.

Tests completed on the Colorado River in Utah have detected the presence of zebra mussel DNA fragments for the first time, the Utah Division of Wildlife Resources announced Tuesday.

"The detection of environmental DNA in the water only indicates the presence of an animal somewhere upstream—it does not confirm that live mussels are present," the DWR stated.

Still, the recent detection shows the serious nature of the threat, as zebra mussels can wreak havoc with an aquatic ecosystem and cause considerable damage.

"Once established, zebra mussels can clog pipes and infrastructure, create recreation hazards on rocks and beaches, and alter ecosystems," said Lt. Bruce Johnson of the Utah Department of Natural Resources Law Enforcement Aquatic Invasive Species Statewide Operations.

"It is critical for anyone who uses boats, paddleboards, kayaks and any other watercraft to adhere to all the laws and to clean, drain and dry their watercraft in order to prevent these aquatic invasive species from spreading further into Utah."

The Utah Division of Wildlife Resources started sampling for invasive mussels in the Colorado River in 2025 from the state line to Moab, Utah.

An environmental DNA autosampler (shown in accompanying photos) was deployed at a new location near the Potash Boat Ramp, about 14 river miles downstream of Moab. Samples were collected daily in June and July.

The U.S. Geological Survey analyzed the water samples and discovered four of the 22 sampled were positive for zebra mussel DNA. Samples collected in the spring and summer from other locations on the Colorado River in Utah did not come back positive.

Also on FTW Outdoors: Fisherman snags paddlefish that avoided capture for 22 years

Those who launch motorized boats in Utah are required to pay an annual aquatic invasive species program vessel enrollment fee, which helps the Department of National Resources operate the state's program to keep the invasive species from spreading around Utah.

Additionally, all river users in Utah—including nonmotorized watercraft such as canoes, paddleboards and rafts—are required to complete Utah's annual mussel-aware boater course .

"As one of the primary users of the Colorado River, nonmotorized boaters are our first line of defense in helping reduce this risk of transporting this species from the Colorado River to other waters in the state," DWR Sportfish Coordinator Trina Hedrick said. "All boaters are encouraged to clean, drain, and dry all watercraft when moving between waterbodies to help prevent the spread of aquatic invasive mussels. There is no time like right now to get serious about this threat."

articles.title: A ketchup bottle cap inspired Princeton engineers to build a shape-shifting robot that moves without a motor
articles.summary: Science News: At Princeton Engineering, a team led by Glaucio Paulino has answered a question few people ever think to ask: what makes a ketchup bottle cap snap ope.
articles.body: At Princeton Engineering, a team led by Glaucio Paulino has answered a question few people ever think to ask: what makes a ketchup bottle cap snap open and stay open rather than flopping shut? The hinge on a typical flip-top ketchup cap attaches a thin, flexible shell to a thicker, rigid base along a curved edge, creating 2 distinct stable positions separated by an energy barrier that the cap must overcome to switch between them. That simple piece of everyday plastic engineering helped reveal something much bigger: how curved, folded shells can hold multiple stable shapes without conventional locking mechanisms. Working from that insight, the team developed mathematical rules for predicting how these structures behave, then used those principles to build a magnetically controlled robot capable of rolling, crawling and changing shape through geometry rather than motors or complex internal mechanisms.How curved-crease origami helped researchers understand the shellsThe study, published June 15, 2026, grew out of work on curved-crease origami, which uses curved folds to turn flat sheets into three-dimensional structures. Unlike ordinary origami, where straight creases are usually the starting point, curved folds can create complicated shapes while allowing a thin sheet to remain lightweight. The researchers first used mathematics to work out how a shell would behave when one of its curved edges was fixed. Their calculations indicated that 2 stable configurations should be possible without stretching the shell. In simple terms, the structure could settle into one shape or another, much like the open and closed positions of a ketchup cap. But the physical models did not behave quite as simply as the equations suggested.Why the researchers found 6 stable shapes instead of 2When the team built and tested the shells, some could settle into 6 or more different stable configurations. The extra shapes appeared because the material developed a narrow band of concentrated deformation that acted much like another crease. The researchers called this feature a pseudocrease. Unlike a crease deliberately put into a sheet, it forms as the structure responds to the forces acting on it. The shell effectively finds another way to bend and settle into a stable position. That unexpected behaviour led the researchers back to their mathematical model. By accounting for the pseudocrease, they were able to explain why the physical structures had more stable states than the original calculation predicted and how the effect changed with the geometry of the shell.How the shells became a robot without a motorThe team then used those different stable positions to make a robot that could change its shape on command. Instead of installing motors and gears inside the machine, the researchers used magnets to trigger transitions between the shell's different configurations. Once a magnetic force pushed the structure past the point where one configuration was stable, the shell could snap into another. The resulting movements allowed the robot to roll and crawl while relying on the structure itself to provide much of the motion. That approach could make certain robots considerably simpler. A conventional moving robot needs motors, gears, batteries and other components to create and control movement. Here, much of that work is built into the shape of the robot before it even moves.Why the ketchup cap connection mattersThe ketchup cap is a simple example of the same principle. Its curved hinge is designed so that the cap has 2 positions it naturally wants to occupy. Pushing the cap past the point between them makes it snap into the other position. The Princeton researchers found that more complicated curved shells can do something similar, but with several possible positions instead of just 2. That gives engineers another way to design objects that can fold, deploy or change shape without adding a complicated mechanical system. The researchers suggest the idea could eventually be useful for reconfigurable structures, deployable architecture and small mechanical devices, as well as robotics. The immediate result, however, is much simpler: a structure inspired by an everyday bottle cap that can change shape and move using magnets, with no motor inside.

articles.body: Elon Muskâs SpaceX has announced its plans to build its largest rocket launch complex in southern Louisiana, a $100 billion project which claims to transform costal wetlands into a critical base for Starship and AI satellite launches. SpaceX posted about this announcement on social media platform X (formerly known as Twitter), âIntroducing Starbase, Louisiana â a high-cadence launch site that will enable Starship to open a pathway to the stars for humanity. Thank you to @LAGovJeffLandry and the great people of Louisiana for all of their support as we work together on this audacious project,â wrote the company. As reported by Reuters, the 125,000-acre site on Pecan Island, named Starbase Louisiana, expands the companyâs Starship operations beyond Texas and Florida as the next-generation rocket nears late-stage development.SpaceX claims Louisiana campus to support thousands of Starship flights annuallyAs reported by Reuters, SpaceX president Gwynne Shotwell said that the upcoming Louisiana campus of the company will eventually support thousands of Starship flights annually, however, the pace depends of overcoming engineering and regulatory hurdles. The company also revealed that the construction for the new SpaceX base will begin from 2029. The âself-sustainingâ spaceport will include methane production for propellant, power generation, deep-water shipping for Starship transport, vehicle processing facilities, and potentially an airport.Environmental and legal contextThe marshland site, more than eight times the size of Manhattan, will preserve large portions of natural wetlands. Shotwell emphasised environmental stewardship, pledging restoration of Pecan Islandâs marshlands and coastline, which serve as natural flood buffers.Jobs and economic impactGovernor Jeff Landry hailed the project as a boost for Louisianaâs economy, promising over 3,000 jobs with average salaries of $92,600, nearly double Vermilion Parishâs median wage. âIt represents jobs for our families, momentum for our communities, and protection for our coast,â Landry said.Strategic role for StarshipThe Louisiana site will be SpaceXâs fourth U.S. launch facility and its second Starbase campus. articles.title: Científicos lo confirma: un estudio asegura que las orcas y delfines han llegado a un punto evolutivo definitivo y jamás volverán a tierra firme
articles.standfirst: Los expertos consideran que han alcanzado un punto de no retorno
articles.summary: Los expertos consideran que han alcanzado un punto de no retorno
articles.body: Hoy en día cuesta creer que algunos mamíferos marinos en algún momento pudieron vivir fuera del agua, lo cierto es que lo hacían. Orcas y delfines son un ejemplo de ello, y es que no fue hasta hace unos 250 millones de años que este tipo de especies se adentraron en el agua para buscar nuevas fuentes de alimento. Ahora, un estudio confirma que, debido a su evolución, ya no hay marcha atrás en esa transición. Un grupo de científicos han publicado un artículo en la revista Proceedings of the Royal Society B y, en este, explican que orcas, delfines y ballenas han alcanzado su punto evolutivo más alto y su estado actual hace imposible que ya no puedan volver a tierra firme en el futuro. El estudio clasifica el grado de adaptación de las especies en cuatro niveles, de los estrictamente terrestres hasta los marinos. Los resultados arrojan una conclusión: aquellas especies semiacuáticas, como castores o nutrias, sí pueden vivir una transición reversible y gradual, pero no así para otros mamíferos marinos. Esta creencia se basa en la Ley de Dollo, que establece que una vez se pierde la estructura anatómica compleja, ya no hay manera de volver a su forma original. A lo largo de los siglos, orcas y delfines han visto cómo cambiaba su cuerpo: atrofia de las extremidades posteriores, el paso de sus patas delanteras a aletas rígidas y el movimiento de su orificio hacia la parte superior del cráneo, entre otros. Todo esto, según el estudio, lleva a la conclusión de que estas especies ya no podrán regresar a tierra firme, ya que no podrían desplazarse o respirar. Además, sus propios cuerpos y la influencia del agua también han jugado un papel esencial. Al cambiar tierra firme por agua, estas especies vieron cómo su masa corporal aumentó y, con ello, tuvieron más grasa para evitar la hipotermia.

articles.title: El desconocido animal que puede tragarse a sus presas enteras, reproducirse en cualquier momento y debe su nombre a un personaje de Disney
articles.standfirst: Habita en las profundidades extremas del océano
articles.summary: Habita en las profundidades extremas del océano
articles.body: Aunque a veces no lo tengamos en cuenta, la realidad es que hay multitud de especies en todo el mundo que no conocemos y que son de lo más curiosas. Por ello, hoy os venimos a hablar del pulpo Dumbo (género Grimpoteuthis), un tierno molusco cefalópodo que habita en las profundidades extremas del océano: concretamente entre los 1.000 y 7.000 metros de profundidad. El primer aspecto llamativo que nos puede fascinar es su nombre, ya que es el mismo que el pequeño elefante volador de Disney, Dumbo. Debe su apodo a las dos aletas laterales de su cabeza, las cuales se asemejan a las grandes orejas del famoso personaje cuando el animal se mueve en el agua. Siguiendo con sus características, también hay que destacar la forma en la que se alimenta. A diferencia de la gran mayoría de los pulpos (que usan su pico para romper y triturar la comida), el pulpo Dumbo engulle a sus presas completamente enteras. Se alimenta principalmente de caracoles, gusanos y pequeños crustáceos que habitan en el fondo marino. Finalmente, al vivir en un entorno abisal con oscuridad perpetua y escasez de recursos, no tiene una época de apareamiento fija. Las hembras cargan con huevos en diferentes etapas de maduración y pueden fertilizarlos y depositarlos individualmente bajo rocas o conchas en cualquier momento del año cuando encuentran un compañero adecuado. Para sobrevivir a la inmensa presión de la zona abisal (que puede ser hasta 700 veces mayor que en la superficie), el pulpo Dumbo ha evolucionado con adaptaciones físicas y biológicas sorprendentes. La clave principal es que su cuerpo está hecho casi por completo de agua y tejido gelatinoso, careciendo de cavidades de aire o estructuras rígidas que puedan ser aplastadas.

articles.title: In 2025, 11-year-old Touren Pope spotted a fossil exposed on the ground in Wyoming; it turned out to be a nearly complete 48-million-year-old turtle shell, and he was allowed to name it
articles.summary: Science News: What began as a routine family rock-hounding trip in southwest Wyoming turned into a paleontological headline when 11-year-old Touren Pope noticed som.
articles.body: What began as a routine family rock-hounding trip in southwest Wyoming turned into a paleontological headline when 11-year-old Touren Pope noticed something unusual poking out of the ground. What heâd spotted was the fossilized shell of a softshell turtle that lived nearly 48 million years ago, preserved in the Bridger Formation of the Greater Green River Basin. After Touren and his grandparents reported the find to the Bureau of Land Management (BLM), experts confirmed its significance and arranged a careful excavation. In recognition of his discovery, Touren was given the rare honor of naming the fossil. Here's the complete story, based on BLM and regional news coverage of the discovery:A keen eye on public landTouren Pope, a sixth-grader from Nevada, was visiting his grandparents in Wyoming in the fall of 2025 when the family set out to search for interesting rocks and minerals on BLM-managed land near Rock Springs. While scanning the ground, he noticed a dark, rounded object that didnât look like an ordinary stone. Following the rules for vertebrate fossils on public land, the family left the specimen in place and contacted the BLM Rock Springs Field Office.BLM paleontology staff quickly recognised the potential importance of the find. J.P. Cavigelli, a paleontologist and museum specialist with the agency, said that within minutes they could tell it was a fairly complete turtle shell worth collecting. Because exposed fossils can deteriorate rapidly once they reach the surface, timing was critical. âIf we donât find them in time, they usually decompose quickly once they reach the surface,â BLM archaeologist Craig Thomas noted.Excavating âLittle TimmyâIn September 2025, a team from the Tate Geological Museum in Casper, working with BLM approval, returned to the site with Touren and his grandparents to fully excavate the fossil.The excavation revealed that only the turtleâs upper shell, or carapace, remained, but it was nearly complete and remarkably well preserved. The shell was carefully transported to the Tate Geological Museum, a BLM-approved repository, where it is being cleaned, stabilized, and prepared for research and possible public display.As a special thank-you, officials allowed Touren to give the fossil an official name. He chose âLittle Timmy,â a moniker that has since appeared in news stories and museum communications about the specimen.By early 2026, Touren even came to the museum to help collections staff clean the fossil, further cementing his connection to the find. A window into a warm, river-filled past During the Eocene Epoch, roughly 48 million years ago, the Greater Green River Basin looked very different than the semi-arid landscape of today. It was much warmer then, with rivers and streams running throughout, supporting a bustling ecosystem of fish, crocodiles, turtles and other animals. Their remains were buried in sediments for millions of years, eventually turning into fossils within rock layers such as the Bridger Formation.Natural erosion later exposed Little Timmyâs shell at the surface, where it waited for someone with a sharp eye to notice. BLM officials say the turtle was likely a softshell species in the trionychid family, whose modern relatives still live in rivers and lakes today. Softshell turtles have flatter, more flexible shells than many other turtles, and their fossils offer clues about ancient aquatic environments and how these animals evolved over time.Why public-land rules matter for fossilsTourenâs discovery also highlights why rules around fossils on public land exist. Vertebrate fossils on BLM-managed areas are considered part of the nationâs scientific and cultural heritage, and removing them without authorization can destroy important context for researchers.By leaving the shell in place and notifying the BLM, Touren and his family ensured that professionals could document the site, collect the specimen properly, and preserve it in a museum where it can be studied and shared with the public.The BLM manages about 245 million acres of public land in the United States, much of it in the West, where erosion constantly exposes new fossils. Agency paleontologists rely on visitors to report potential finds so that significant specimens arenât lost to weather, vandalism, or unregulated collecting. In that sense, Tourenâs story is both a personal triumph and a model for how the public can help protect ancient history.From rock hound to fossil namesakeFor an 11-year-old, being credited with uncovering a 48-million-year-old turtle is extraordinary. For scientists, Little Timmy is a valuable data point in reconstructing the Eocene ecosystems of the Green River Basin.And for the museums, the specimen is a future exhibit that can inspire other young rock hounds to carefully examine the ground underfoot. Tourenâs discovery reminds us that significant scientific contributions arenât always made in university labs or with large field crews. Sometimes, they begin with a curious kid, a family outing, and the choice to do the right thing when something ancient and fragile emerges from the dirt.

articles.title: 1,500-year-old child burial unearthed in Peru with whistles, a rattle and a striking sculptural vessel, archaeologists uncover clues to an ancient civilisationâs rituals
articles.summary: Science News: Archaeologists working at the Huacas de Moche Archaeological Complex in northern Peru have uncovered the burial of an infant estimated to be about 1,5.
articles.body: Archaeologists working at the Huacas de Moche Archaeological Complex in northern Peru have uncovered the burial of an infant estimated to be about 1,500 years old. The child, approximately 1.5 years old, was buried with a funerary assemblage that included two whistles, a rattle and a sculptural vessel. Researchers say the burial displays a pattern characteristic of the Moche culture. According to Peru's Andina news agency, archaeologists discovered the burial in Architectural Complex 61, located in the southern sector of the Moche urban core. Archaeologist Jermi Mejia said the infant's remains were found in a reclining position, with the head facing south and the legs facing north.A carefully arranged burialMejia said the burial was accompanied by four notable objects: two whistles, a rattle and a sculptural vessel. These items provide information about the cultural and funerary practices of the society that inhabited the site around 1,500 years ago. The objects also give archaeologists an opportunity to examine how funerary items were placed alongside the dead. Their exact significance to the Moche, however, cannot be determined from the discovery alone.The burial's location and arrangement add to the archaeological evidence from the site, allowing researchers to examine how funerary practices were carried out within the Moche urban environment.Found in a residential areaThe location of the burial is just as important as the objects found with it. Architectural Complex 61 is situated in the southern sector of the Moche urban core and contains small platforms and partition walls that separated spaces used for different activities. Archaeologists also recovered domestic vessels associated with the abandonment of the space. According to Andina, these objects provide insights into aspects of diet, daily activities and the use of residential areas.That combination of domestic evidence and a child burial gives researchers an opportunity to look beyond the ceremonial spaces of Huacas de Moche. Instead, the excavation is helping researchers examine aspects of life within the residential parts of the ancient settlement. The excavation work includes graphic, elevation, photographic, film and aerial documentation. Researchers will also continue excavating deeper levels to identify changes made to the architecture over time.Understanding the Moche communityThe Huacas de Moche Archaeological Project is focused on expanding knowledge about the population that inhabited the Moche urban core and understanding their daily lives beyond ceremonial spaces, according to project director Carlos Rengifo. The current field season includes three main areas of work: the ceremonial and funerary area, the urban, domestic and residential sector, and production areas.The Huacas de Moche Archaeological Project was established in 1991 as an academic research initiative led by National University of Trujillo faculty members Santiago Uceda and Ricardo Morales. Its study area encompasses the Huacas del Sol y la Luna and the spaces associated with the surrounding adobe structures. The research is funded by the National University of Trujillo, which has supported the project since its creation. The project also includes conservation, tourism and community outreach activities.More clues beneath the surfaceThe newly uncovered burial is part of a wider excavation effort at the archaeological complex. The current stage of work is expected to continue for approximately one month, after which the area will be protected with clean sand against possible rainfall associated with the El Niño phenomenon. The excavation is helping researchers build a broader picture of the people who lived at Huacas de Moche. While the site is widely associated with its monumental adobe structures, investigations of residential and domestic spaces can provide different clues about everyday life. The infant's burial adds another piece to that picture. Its location, orientation and accompanying objects provide archaeologists with evidence of funerary practices within the Moche urban core.The whistles, rattle and sculptural vessel cannot by themselves reveal exactly what the Moche intended when they were placed beside the child. But together with the burial's characteristic arrangement, they provide researchers with additional evidence for studying the cultural and funerary practices of the society that inhabited Huacas de Moche around 1,500 years ago.
